# Figures and layout {short-title="Figures"}

This chapter documents the insertion of static figures, the generation of figures from
Python code, multi-column layout, and the special case of PDF-only figures (TikZ,
PGFplots).

## Static image with caption and cross-reference {#sec-fig-static}

The basic syntax for inserting an image is:

````markdown
![Figure caption.](../../images/my-image.png){#fig-label width=80%}
````

The identifier `#fig-label` allows a cross-reference with `@fig-label`.
The `width` attribute accepts percentages or absolute values (`5cm`, `0.5\linewidth`).

Here is an example with the {{< acrs cnam >}} logo:

````markdown
![The official Cnam logo.](../../images/Cnam.jpg){#fig-logo-cnam width=40%}
````

![The official {{< acrs cnam >}} logo.](../../images/Cnam.jpg){#fig-logo-cnam width=40%}

@fig-logo-cnam shows the official {{< acrs cnam >}} logo, loaded from the `images/`
folder at the project root.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Recommended image formats

- **PDF**: prefer vector formats `.pdf` or `.eps` for diagrams and charts (sharp at
  all resolutions). For photographs, `.png` or `.jpg` at 300 dpi minimum.
- **HTML**: all standard web formats (`.png`, `.jpg`, `.svg`). `.svg` files are
  particularly well suited for diagrams.
- Quarto automatically handles format conversion depending on the render target.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Paths are relative to the `.qmd` file, not to the project root

Image paths are relative to the location of the `.qmd` file. From
`content_en/chapters/`, the `images/` folder at the project root is at
`../../images/myfile.png`. This behaviour is identical in PDF and HTML.
:::

## Python-generated figures {#sec-fig-python}

Quarto can execute Python cells (via Jupyter) and include their graphical output as
numbered figures. The chunk syntax uses options prefixed with `#|`:

````markdown
```{{python}}
#| label: fig-sincos
#| fig-cap: "Curves $\\sin(x)$ and $\\cos(x)$ over $[0, 2\\pi]$."
#| echo: true
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 300)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3))
axes[0].plot(x, np.sin(x), color='#d20025')
axes[0].set_title(r'$\sin(x)$')
axes[1].plot(x, np.cos(x), color='#005EA5')
axes[1].set_title(r'$\cos(x)$')
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel('$x$')
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
```
````

::: {.render-demo}
**Output:**

```{python}
#| label: fig-sincos
#| fig-cap: "Curves $\\sin(x)$ and $\\cos(x)$ over $[0, 2\\pi]$."
#| echo: true
#| fig-pos: 'H'
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 300)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3))
axes[0].plot(x, np.sin(x), color='#d20025')
axes[0].set_title(r'$\sin(x)$')
axes[1].plot(x, np.cos(x), color='#005EA5')
axes[1].set_title(r'$\cos(x)$')
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel('$x$')
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
```

:::

@fig-sincos is generated at each compilation. With `execute: freeze: auto` in
`_quarto.yml`, Quarto caches the results in `_freeze/` and only re-executes the code
if the chunk has changed — useful for figures that take a long time to compute.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `plt.tight_layout()` is essential

Without `plt.tight_layout()`, axis labels frequently overlap in the PDF. Always end
your matplotlib figures with this line.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## `echo: false` for the final document

During writing, `echo: true` displays the code — convenient for review. For the
version submitted to the doctoral school, switch figure chunks to `#| echo: false`
to display only the graphic.
:::

## Multi-column layout {#sec-multicol}

The `layout-ncol` directive places several figures side by side. Apply it to a div
containing sub-figures:

````markdown
::: {#fig-duo layout-ncol=2}

```{{python}}
#| label: fig-duo-a
#| fig-cap: "Function $x^2$"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, numpy as np
x = np.linspace(-2, 2, 200)
plt.plot(x, x**2, color='#d20025'); plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3); plt.tight_layout()
```

```{{python}}
#| label: fig-duo-b
#| fig-cap: "Function $\\sqrt{|x|}$"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, numpy as np
x = np.linspace(-2, 2, 200)
plt.plot(x, np.sqrt(np.abs(x)), color='#005EA5'); plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3); plt.tight_layout()
```

Two elementary functions.
:::
````

::: {.render-demo}
**Output:**

::: {#fig-duo layout-ncol=2 fig-pos='H'}

```{python}
#| label: fig-duo-a
#| fig-cap: "Function $x^2$"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, numpy as np
x = np.linspace(-2, 2, 200)
plt.plot(x, x**2, color='#d20025'); plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3); plt.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-duo-b
#| fig-cap: "Function $\\sqrt{|x|}$"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, numpy as np
x = np.linspace(-2, 2, 200)
plt.plot(x, np.sqrt(np.abs(x)), color='#005EA5'); plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3); plt.tight_layout()
```

Two elementary functions.
:::

:::

@fig-duo groups the two sub-figures @fig-duo-a and @fig-duo-b. The last line of text
in the div becomes the overall caption.

## PDF-only figures (TikZ, PGFplots) {#sec-fig-latex}

Some complex figures can only be generated in LaTeX (TikZ, PGFplots,
`circuitikz`…). They are inserted via a `{=latex}` block inside a figure div,
accompanied by replacement content visible in HTML:

````markdown
:::{#fig-tikz fig-pos='h'}
```{=latex}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}
  \draw[thick, ->] (0,0) -- (3,0) node[right] {$x$};
  \draw[thick, ->] (0,0) -- (0,2) node[above] {$y$};
  \draw[blue, thick] plot[domain=0:2.8, samples=50] (\x, {sin(\x r)});
\end{tikzpicture}
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
*(TikZ figure — available in the PDF version only)*
:::

Example TikZ figure inserted as raw LaTeX.
:::
````

::: {.render-demo}
**Output:**

:::{#fig-tikz fig-pos='H'}
```{=latex}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}
  \draw[thick, ->] (0,0) -- (3,0) node[right] {$x$};
  \draw[thick, ->] (0,0) -- (0,2) node[above] {$y$};
  \draw[blue, thick] plot[domain=0:2.8, samples=50] (\x, {sin(\x r)});
\end{tikzpicture}
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
*(TikZ figure — available in the PDF version only)*
:::

Example TikZ figure inserted as raw LaTeX.
:::

:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Alternative: compile the TikZ figure as a separate PDF

For complex TikZ figures, a more robust approach is to compile them as a standalone
`.pdf` file, then include them as a regular image:

```markdown
![Caption.](figures/my-tikz-diagram.pdf){#fig-tikz width=80%}
```

This avoids package conflicts and speeds up compilation.
:::

## Float positioning (PDF) {#sec-float-pos}

In LaTeX, figures and tables are *floats*: LaTeX decides their position to achieve the
best possible layout. The `fig-pos` attribute (figures) or `tbl-pos` (tables) allows
you to give it instructions.

````markdown
![Caption.](../../images/Cnam.jpg){#fig-ex fig-pos='tb'}
````

Specifiers can be freely combined in a string:

| Specifier | Meaning |
|:---:|:---|
| `h` | *here* — at the exact point in the text (if space allows) |
| `t` | *top* — at the top of the current or next page |
| `b` | *bottom* — at the bottom of the current or next page |
| `p` | *page* — on a page dedicated to floats |
| `!` | Ignores LaTeX's internal constraints (density, float count) |
| `H` | Forces placement *here*, without any floating (requires `\usepackage{float}`) |

The default value in Quarto is `tbp`. For a Python chunk, the specifier is passed as
a cell option:

````markdown
```{{python}}
#| label: fig-python
#| fig-cap: "My figure."
#| fig-pos: 'h'
```
````

To set a default specifier for the entire document, add to `_quarto.yml`:

````yaml
fig-pos: 'H'
````

::: {.callout-warning}
## `h` is not a guarantee

The `h` specifier asks LaTeX to place the float *here if possible*, but LaTeX may
ignore it if there is insufficient space. The combination `ht` (here, then top of page)
is generally more robust. `H` forces placement unconditionally, but can create nearly
empty pages if the figure is large — reserve it for cases where position is truly
critical.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Floats only apply to PDF

In HTML, `fig-pos` and `tbl-pos` are ignored: figures and tables are inserted in the
document flow at their insertion point, like any other element.
:::
